docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The goal of the Altair 8800 Z80 AI Edition is to blend the old with the new — using AI to help you build software for the Altair 8800 running on the ESP32-S3, Linux/macOS, Windows, and Docker. You'll pick up computing fundamentals and learn how to work alongside AI tools to write code for a 1970s computer.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text:
This project stands on the shoulders of the following projects:

  1. A complete emulation of the Intel 8080 processor written in C99.
  2. Deramp retro disks.
  3. The Altair Front Panel Kit.
  4. CP/M Disk Operating System.
  5. CP/M-80 2.2 Compilers and Retro Compiler Community
  6. Codex and Claude Foundation models.

docs.title: Agentic Engineering
docs.text:
You may have heard of "vibe coding" — tossing a quick request at an AI and hoping for the best. Agentic engineering is the grown-up version. AI doesn't do the thinking for you: you still need to understand the problem and steer it towards designs that, in our case, fit a tiny computer with very little memory. Think of the AI as a fast but eager helper — it writes a lot of the code, but you stay in charge, deciding how the project is structured, setting the rules it follows, and reviewing everything to make sure it actually works.

It's a more demanding way of working than firing off prompts and hoping — and it rewards the same habits good engineers already rely on. Plan before you build: sketch out what you want and agree the approach with the AI first, then let it write the code. Work in small, testable steps so problems are easy to spot, and review everything it produces rather than accepting code you don't understand. Do that and you'll learn plenty, not just about the Altair 8800, but about how to build real software alongside AI.

Want to dig deeper? Start with Simon Willison's post on Vibe Engineering and Andrew Orobator's Vibe Engineering: From Random Code to Deterministic Systems.

docs.title: The Altair 8800 Personal Computer
docs.text:
The Altair 8800 kick-started the personal computer revolution. Microsoft's first product was Altair BASIC written for the Altair 8800 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen. At the time, Altair BASIC was a huge step forward as it allowed people to write programs using a high-level programming language.

The Altair project provides a fun way to learn:

  1. Agentic engineer Altair 8800 applications using Intel 8080 Assembly, BDS C, and Microsoft BASIC, with help from Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Claude Sonnet or OpenAI Codex, in VS Code with GitHub Copilot.
  2. Learn to build multithreaded, event-driven IoT C applications that scale from microcontrollers and Raspberry Pis to desktop-class computers.
  3. Safely explore machine-level programming, including Intel 8080 Assembly, C, and BASIC development.
  4. Chat with AI directly from the Altair, using OpenAI cloud models or GenAI models hosted locally with Ollama or LM Studio.
  5. Enjoy retro gaming and play classic games from the past.
  6. Optionally, integrate free weather and pollution cloud services from Open Weather Map.

docs.text:
The Altair emulator runs in three main ways:

  1. ESP32-S3 microcontroller boards — the primary, most interesting target. The emulator runs natively on ESP32-S3 boards with a physical Altair front panel, VT100 or TFT LCD display output, SD-card disk storage, WiFi, and a WebSocket browser terminal.
  2. Desktop — compile and run the emulator natively on POSIX compatible operating systems including Linux, ChromeOS, Windows with WSL 2, and macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel.
  3. Apple container — run the SBC emulator with a browser terminal and host sound on an Apple silicon Mac.

docs.title: Altair history
docs.text:
Altair 8800 image attribution - Smithsonian Museum

The Altair 8800 was built on the Intel 8080 CPU, the second 8-bit microprocessor manufactured by Intel in 1974. By today's standards, it's a simple CPU design, perfect for learning computing fundamentals because of its small instruction set.

The original Altair 8800 was programmed by setting switches on the front panel. It was a painstaking, error-prone process to load and run a program. The Altair 8800 had a series of LEDs and switches that you used to load apps and determine the state of the Altair.

You could save and load applications from a paper tape reader connected to the Altair 8800. As the Altair 8800 grew in popularity, more options became available. You could attach a keyboard, a computer monitor, and finally disk drives, a more reliable way to save and load applications.

There are three components to the Altair 8800 emulator solution.

  1. The Altair Web Terminal
  2. The Altair emulator
  3. Cloud services

docs.title: Deployment Options
docs.text:
There are three ways to deploy the Altair 8800 emulator.

  1. Run in an Apple container
  2. Build from source
  3. Deploy on Azure Sphere

docs.title: Apple container
docs.text: The Apple container runs the SBC emulator on macOS, with a browser terminal and host sound. See Apple container.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
You can also build the Altair emulator from the source code and run it as a native application on your computer. For more information, refer to Compiling the Altair emulator.

Reasons to do this include:

  1. You want to make changes to the Altair emulator code.
  2. You want to run the emulator natively.
  3. You'd want to learn how to build the Altair emulator from the source code.
  4. You have an Apple Silicon Mac and want to run the Altair emulator natively on one of the Apple Silicon efficiency cores.

Building the Altair 8800 emulator from source has been tested and is supported on the following POSIX compatible operating systems.

  • Windows 11 with WSL 2
  • Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04
  • macOS,
  • Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit (preferred) and 32-bit

docs.title: Azure Sphere
docs.text:
If you have an Azure Sphere device, you can run the Altair 8800 emulator on it. The Altair emulator runs as a native application on the Azure Sphere device. The Altair emulator is a POSIX compatible application and runs on the Azure Sphere OS.

Follow the Deploy on Azure Sphere instructions.

docs.title: The Emulator
docs.text:
The Altair 8800 emulator is a software program that emulates the Altair 8800 computer. The Altair emulator is written in C and runs on most desktop operating systems as well as devices like the Raspberry Pi, Beaglebone, and Azure Sphere.

This is version 5 of the Altair 8800 emulator project and it shares a similar code base as the Azure Sphere Cloud-Enabled Altair 8800 as featured on the Register "Microsoft adds cloud enablement to 1970s Altair 8800 tech".

docs.title: Source code
docs.text:
• The Altair emulator source code is maintained in the Altair 8800 Emulator GitHub repo.
  • The soltion is Open Source and is provided under an MIT License, and contributions are very welcome.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The Altair emulator runs on POSIX compatible operating systems including, Linux, Windows with WSL 2, macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel, as well as devices like Raspberry Pi, Beaglebone, and Azure Sphere.

Starting from the bottom left and moving up and then to the right.

  • POSIX Compatible OS:. The Altair 8800 emulator runs on POSIX compatible operating systems, including Linux, macOS, Windows WSL 2, and Raspberry Pi OS.
  • WebSocket & MQTT C: These communication libraries connect the Altair emulator to the web terminal and cloud services. The Altair terminal IO messages are routed over WebSockets, and the IoT data over MQTT.
  • Event library: The Altair coordinates activities on the main thread using the event event loop library.
  • EdgeDevX: This library simplifies access to Azure IoT services, provides event-timer services, along with several useful utilities.
  • Terminal IO & Cloud Services: The Intel 8080 CPU provides 256 input ports and 256 output ports. The Intel 8080 ports were used to integrate peripherals such as disk drives, printers, and modems. However, for the Altair emulator, these ports are used to integrate communications and cloud services. Terminal input and output ports are routed over WebSockets, other ports are used for timing services, access to weather and pollution data, plus Azure IoT services.
  • Intel 8080 emulator: This is an open-source software implementation of the Intel 8080 CPU. The Intel 8080 emulator executes Intel 8080 applications including the CP/M operating system, compilers, apps, and games.
  • CPU Monitor: The CPU monitor implements the virtual Altair front panel, along with memory disassembler, tracer, and Altair emulator reset.
  • CP/M: CP/M originally stood for Control Program/Monitor. Later, CP/M became known as Control Program for Microcomputers. It was a mass-market operating system created in 1974 for Intel 8080/85-based microcomputers by Gary Kildall of Digital Research, Inc.
  • Programming languages: Included on the main disk image are the Microsoft BASIC interpreter, the BDS C compiler, and the Intel and Microsoft assemblers and linkers.
  • Altair BASIC: By default the Altair emulator boots CP/M, but it is easy to boot the original Altair BASIC program.
  • Altair Web Terminal: Provides a web-browser hosted Altair terminal. The web terminal is built using the Xterm library. Xterm.js provides a web browser-hosted terminal, a WebSocket integrates Xterm with the Altair emulator.
  • Open Weather Map: Open Weather Map provides planet-scale weather and pollution data services. Open Weather Map provides free access to weather and pollution data by geographic location.
  • ThingsBoard: ThingsBoard is an open-source IoT platform for data collection, processing, visualization, and device management. ThingsBoard supports industry-standard IoT protocols: MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP. The Altair emulator uses the MQTT protocol to connect to ThingsBoard.

docs.title: Start the Web Terminal
docs.text:
The Altair web terminal is a remote terminal command prompt for the Altair emulator. The web terminal is a static web app and is hosted in your web browser and connects to the Altair emulator. When the web terminal connects, the Altair terminal reports the emulator and CP/M versions, and you can start to use the Altair.

Note, there are links on the web terminal to the retro games GitHub repo, the documentation, and user and programming manuals.

docs.title: Learn about CP/M
docs.text:
CP/M originally stood for Control Program/Monitor. Later, CP/M became known as Control Program for Microcomputers. It was a mass-market operating system created in 1974 for Intel 8080/85-based microcomputers by Gary Kildall of Digital Research, Inc.

The first version was single-tasking on 8-bit processors with support for up to 64 kilobytes of memory. Later versions of CP/M added multiple-user variations and were migrated to 16-bit processors.

For more information about CP/M, see the CP/M Wikipedia article and CP/M Frequently Asked Questions.

docs.title: Digital Research CP/M Operating System Manual
docs.text: You will find a wealth of information about CP/M, including compilers, assemblers, debuggers, and more in the Digital Research CP/M Operating System Manual

docs.title: Programming the Altair emulator
docs.text: From CP/M, you can program the Altair emulator using Microsoft BASIC, BD Software C, the Intel Assembler and Linker, and the Microsoft MACRO-80 Assembler.

docs.title: Get started with CP/M
docs.text:
Here are some CP/M commands to get you started:

  • Changing drives. The Altair emulator mounts two drives, drive A and drive B. To change drives, from the Altair CP/M command prompt in the Web Terminal, type the drive name, then press the Enter key.

    a:

b:

  • Display a directory listing.

    dir

dir *.BAS

ls

  • Erase a file.

    era *.txt

  • Copy Microsoft BASIC mbasic.com from drive A to drive B.

    a:pip b:mbasic.com.com=a:mbasic.com

  • List the contents of a file.

    type lunar.bas

  • Rename a file.

    ren lander.bas=lunar.bas

  3. Start the game from the CP/M command line:

docs.title: Rebooting the Emulator
docs.text:
There are various reasons why you might want to reboot the Altair operating system.

  1. You may crash the Altair operating system if you hack the current CPU instruction pointer or corrupt RAM. You might corrupt memory while programming in Assembly or with the virtual front panel.
  2. You might have tried to access a drive letter that is not available. The only way to recover is to reboot the Altair.
  3. You want to boot Altair BASIC and run the original Altair BASIC written by Bill Gates and Paul Allan.

You'll be glad to know it's easy to reboot the Altair.

docs.title: Reboot CP/M
docs.text:
1. From the web terminal, select Ctrl+M to enter the CPU monitor.
  2. Type r (for Altair RESET), followed by Enter to boot CP/M.

docs.title: Reboot Altair BASIC
docs.text:
By default, the Altair emulator loads CP/M on startup. To load Altair BASIC, follow these instructions.

  1. From the web terminal, select Ctrl+M to enter the CPU monitor.
  2. Type basic (for Altair BASIC), followed by Enter to boot Altair BASIC.

  3. You'll be prompted for the following information:

    • MEMORY SIZE?: Select the Enter key to accept the default.
    • TERMINAL WIDTH?: Select Enter to accept the default.
    • WANT SIN-COS-TAN-ATN?: Enter Y or N.

    Altair BASIC responds with the amount of memory and version information.

For more information about Altair BASIC, refer to Altair-BASIC-programming

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Adding cloud services to the Altair 8800 emulator is optional, but it does provide some interesting features such as internet weather and pollution data, and the ability to report Altair 8800 telemetry to an MQTT broker.

You can use the following cloud services with the Altair emulator.

  • Open Weather Map provides planet-scale weather and pollution data services. Open Weather Map provides free access to weather and pollution data.

docs.title: Open Weather Map
docs.text: Connecting the Open Weather Map cloud service is optional, free, and recommended so the Altair emulator can stream weather and pollution information over MQTT.

docs.title: Create an Open Weather Map API Key
docs.text:
1. From your web browser navigate to https://openweathermap.org/api
  2. Sign in to Open Weather Map
  3. Select API from the Open Weather Map main menu.
  4. Subscribe to the Current Weather Data. Select the Free option, and select Get API key.
  5. Repeat and subscribe to the Air Pollution API. Select the Free option, and select Get API key.
  6. Select API Keys from the Open Weather Map site.
  7. Copy the Open Weather Map API key somewhere safe as you will need this data when you start the Altair in cloud-connected mode.

docs.title: Open Weather Map air quality calculation
docs.text:
Open Weather Map air quality calculation is based on the Common Air Quality Index (CAQI). The Common Air Quality Index (CAQI) is an air quality index used in Europe since 2006.

For more information, refer to the calculation of Air Quality index.

docs.title: About Azure IoT Central
docs.text:
Connecting Azure IoT Central is optional and free to try. IoT Central will be very useful as you can stream and report weather, pollution, and diagnostics data, as well as export data for anomaly detection.

In this exercise, you will create an Azure IoT Central application. Later you will learn about Altair applications that stream data to Azure IoT Central. Applications that stream data to Azure IoT Central include WEATHER.BAS and JSON.BAS.

docs.title: Azure IoT Central
docs.text:
Azure IoT Central is a cloud-based Internet of Things (IoT) application platform. It provides an easy way to connect, monitor, and manage your IoT assets at scale. Azure IoT Central builds on Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service, Stream Analytics, and Time Series Insights.

Azure IoT Central follows the eight attributes of successful IoT solutions.

docs.title: IoT Plug and Play
docs.text:
This solution uses IoT Plug and Play with IoT Central. IoT Plug and Play (PnP) defines a model that a device uses to advertise its capabilities to a PnP-enabled application like IoT Central. PnP is an open specification, to learn more, refer to What is IoT Plug and Play.

An IoT Plug and Play CO2 monitor model has been published to the public repository of IoT Plug and Play models. A local copy of the IoT Plug and Play model is located in the iot_plug_and_play directory.

When your device first connects to IoT Central, the IoT Plug and Play model is retrieved from the public repository of models. IoT Central then creates default views using the Plug and Play model.

The IoT Plug and Play model for the CO2 monitor project is declared in main.h.

#define IOT_PLUG_AND_PLAY_MODEL_ID "dtmi:com:example:azuresphere:co2monitor;2"

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Run the Z80 ROMless SBC emulator in an Apple container on macOS, with a browser terminal and a native sound client. The container uses banked CP/M 2.2 and four 512 KiB disks mounted from this project's disks/512kb directory.

Install the prerequisites, then start the container and sound client together.

docs.title: Build Container Image
docs.text:
The launcher builds the local Apple container image and the host sound client:

python3 docker/start.py

The shared image contains the SBC emulator and browser terminal. Build the image and host sound client without launching it:

python3 scripts/z80_container.py prepare

The shared repository's sound client uses miniaudio for audio output. Container orchestration currently targets Apple containers on macOS.

docs.title: Install Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Apple's container CLI on an Apple silicon Mac, plus Python 3, CMake and a C compiler. The shared container is the external/z80-cpm-container submodule. Set Z80_CPM_CONTAINER to an alternate checkout when needed. Initialize the project submodules:

git submodule update --init --recursive
container system start

The first build needs network access for Debian packages and the miniaudio header. An audio output device is required by the host sound client.

docs.title: Start the Emulator
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

python3 scripts/z80_container.py start

Or run the VS Code task Run interactive CP/M emulator. CP/M boots in the task terminal. Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ to give the browser exclusive control; it returns to the task terminal when the browser disconnects. Press Enter after a handover to display the current prompt. Ctrl+] in the task terminal stops the sound client and removes the container. Ctrl+C is sent to CP/M so MBASIC can use it to interrupt a BASIC program.

Before CP/M starts, all four disks/512kb/ images are checked for exact 512 KiB size and filesystem integrity using the container's fsck.cpm -n. Failure reports the disk and checker output, stops startup and leaves images unchanged; the checker does not repair filesystems. Successful validation messages for A-D appear in the task terminal before the CP/M prompt.

The project's disks/512kb is always mounted read/write. Drive A boot tracks and AUTORUN.COM are refreshed on startup; other files persist. These are the same base disks used by Apps/build-all.ps1, not temporary session copies. You can edit, create and delete files from CP/M, then stop with Ctrl+] in the task terminal. Stop the emulator before host-side builds or disk copies. See editing and copying base disks to the Z80 SBC for build-and-copy, copy-only and VS Code tasks.

--web-port, --sound-port and --console-port choose different localhost ports; --skip-build reuses the existing image.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This is version 5 of the Azure Sphere Altair Emulator and shares the same code base as the Altair 8800 docker project that runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: Source code
docs.text:
• The Altair on Azure Sphere source code is maintained at AI and Cloud powered Altair 8800
  • The Altair Front Panel hardware design.
  • All the source is provided under an MIT License, and contributions are very welcome.

docs.title: Azure Sphere
docs.text:
Azure Sphere is a secure embedded platform that is ideal for quickly developing an IoT system. By providing a platform meeting all 7 properties of highly secured devices, Azure Sphere eliminates the need to be a hardware, OS, and security expert. These seven properties make Azure Sphere ideal for running Intelligent Edge solutions.

Azure Sphere consists of the following components:

  • Azure Sphere–certified chips from hardware partners include built-in Microsoft security technology to provide connectivity and a dependable hardware root of trust.
  • Azure Sphere OS adds layers of protection and ongoing security updates to create a trustworthy platform for new IoT experiences.
  • Azure Sphere Security Service brokers trust for device-to-cloud communication, detects threats and renews device security.

docs.title: Altair on Azure Sphere
docs.text: The Altair emulator is supported on Azure Sphere devices from Avnet and Seeed Studio. If an Azure Sphere device is paired with the Altair front panel kit or the Mikroe Altair Retro Click, the Altair address and data bus activity are displayed.

docs.title: Ideal Azure Sphere config
docs.text:
The ideal Azure Sphere configuration is the Avnet Azure Sphere Starter Kit paired with the MikroE microSD Click and the MikroE 8800 Retro Click.

Azure Sphere with the Altair front panel kit MikroE Retro Click

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The Altair solution is deployed across all three custom app cores on Azure Sphere, including two workloads on the low-power real-time cores. The Altair emulator runs on the high-level Cortex A7 core, a continuous movement classification TinyML model runs on one of the real-time cores, and the other real-time core runs storage services.

Starting from the bottom left and moving up and then to the right.

  • WebSocket & Azure IoT C: These communication libraries connect the Altair emulator to the web terminal and cloud services. The Altair terminal IO messages are routed over WebSockets, and the Azure IoT C SDK connects the Altair to Azure IoT Central.
  • Event loop: The Altair coordinates activities on the main thread using the built-in Event loop library.
  • AzureSphereDevX: This library simplifies access to Azure IoT services, and provides event-timer services, along with several useful utilities.
  • Terminal IO & Cloud Services: The Intel 8080 CPU provides 256 input ports and 256 output ports. The Intel 8080 ports were used to integrate peripherals such as disk drives, printers, and modems. However, for the Altair emulator, these ports are used to integrate communications and cloud services. Terminal input and output ports are routed over WebSockets, other ports are used for timing services, access to weather and pollution data, plus Azure IoT services.
  • Intel 8080 emulator: This is an open-source software implementation of the Intel 8080 CPU. The Intel 8080 emulator executes Intel 8080 applications including the CP/M operating system, compilers, apps, and games.
  • CPU Monitor: The CPU monitor implements the virtual Altair front panel, along with memory disassembler, tracer, and Altair emulator reset.
  • CP/M: CP/M originally stood for Control Program/Monitor. Later, CP/M became known as Control Program for Microcomputers. It was a mass-market operating system created in 1974 for Intel 8080/85-based microcomputers by Gary Kildall of Digital Research, Inc.
  • Programming languages: Included on the main disk image are the Microsoft BASIC interpreter, the BDS C compiler, and the Intel and Microsoft assemblers and linkers.
  • Altair BASIC: By default the Altair emulator boots CP/M, but it is easy to boot the original Altair BASIC program.
  • Altair Web Terminal: Provides a web-browser-hosted Altair terminal. The web terminal is built using the Xterm library. Xterm.js provides a web browser-hosted terminal, a WebSocket integrates Xterm with the Altair emulator.
  • Open Weather Map: Open Weather Map provides planet-scale weather and pollution data services. Open Weather Map provides free access to weather and pollution data by geographic location.
  • ThingsBoard: ThingsBoard is an open-source IoT platform for data collection, processing, visualization, and device management. ThingsBoard supports industry-standard IoT protocols: MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP. The Altair emulator uses the MQTT protocol to connect to ThingsBoard.

docs.title: Backup an Altair boot SD card
docs.text:
You've been creating apps from the Altair emulator and saving them to the CP/M filesystem. Now you want to backup the contents of the SD card and recreate Altair disk images from the backup.

To create a backup, you extract the Altair SD card contents to a binary file. Then you separate the backup file into individual Altair disk images.

The process is:

  1. Remove the SD card from the Azure Sphere device and plug it into your computer.
  2. Open a command prompt and navigate to the Altair_sd_card_image_tools folder.
  3. Power off the Azure Sphere device.

  4. Extract the SD card contents to a binary file.

    • On Linux and macOS, run the DD command.

      sudo dd if=/dev/sda of=altair_extracted_sd_card_image.bin bs=512 count=12000; sync

    • On Windows, download and run dd.

      List the Windows disks.

      dd --list

      The following command assumes the SD card is mounted as the D: drive. Adjust the drive letter to be used based on your Windows disk configuration.

      dd if=\\.\d: of=altair_extracted_sd_card_image.bin bs=512 count=12000

    This will read the SD card into a file named altair_extracted_sd_card_image.bin.

docs.title: Extract Altair disk images from a backup
docs.text:
1. Run the following command to extract Altair disk images from a SD card backup image.

    python3 extract_disks_from_sd_card_image.py

    Using the default settings, the extract_disks_from_sd_card_image.py script will create four Altair disk images.

    - azsphere_cpm63k.dsk
- bdsc-v1.60.dsk
- escape.dsk
- blank.dsk

docs.title: Create an Altair boot disk image from disk images
docs.text:
Altair disk images can be used to create an Altair boot image to be flashed to an SD card.

To create an SD card binary image from Altair disk images, run the following command:

create_sd_card_image_from_disks.py

By default, the create_sd_card_image_from_disks.py Python script will create a binary disk image file named altair_burn_disk_image.bin from the following disk images:

- azsphere_cpm63k.dsk
- bdsc-v1.60.dsk
- escape.dsk
- blank.dsk

docs.title: Power Management
docs.text: The Altair running on Azure Sphere takes advantage of advanced power management features to reduce power consumption.

docs.title: Automatic sleep
docs.text:
By default, the Altair emulator will auto sleep after 10 minutes of no terminal activity. Sleep will halt the Intel 8080 CPU emulator, disable WiFi, and place the Azure Sphere in low performance mode.

To wake the emulator, press button B on the Azure Sphere Developer Kit.

docs.title: Power management settings
docs.text: The following table describes how to use the power management settings. From the CP/M command prompt, run the power command.

docs.title: The CP/M power command
docs.text: Command Description power d Disable power management power e Enable power management power s Force to the Altair to sleep

docs.title: i8080 power management IO ports
docs.text:
The power management IO ports are used to control the power management settings. See the i8080 Azure Sphere specific ports for information on how to use the IO ports

The power management IO ports can be used to control the power management settings from your custom Altair applications. The following code snippets show how to control the power management.

These examples first disable the power management, then enable the power management, then set wake from sleep to 10 seconds, then force the Altair to sleep.

docs.title: C code
docs.text:
outp(66, 0x00);     // Disable power management
outp(66, 0x01);     // Enable power management
outp(67, 10);       // Wake from sleep after 10 seconds
outp(66, 0x02);     // Force to the Altair to sleep

docs.title: Microsoft BASIC code
docs.text:
10 OUT 66, 0:   REM Disable power management
20 OUT 66, 1:   REM Enable power management
30 OUT 67, 10:  REM Wake from sleep after 10 seconds
40 OUT 66, 2:   REM Force to the Altair to sleep

docs.title: Assembly code
docs.text:
ORG 0100H   ;CP/M base of TPA (transient program area)
MVI A,0     ;Disable power management
OUT 66      ;Call sleep port

MVI A,1     ;Enable power management
OUT 66      ;Call sleep port

MVI A,10    ;Wake from sleep after 10 seconds
OUT 67      ;Call wake from sleep port

MVI A,2     ;Force sleep
OUT 66      ;Call sleep port

RET

docs.text:
The Altair web terminal is a remote terminal command prompt for the Altair emulator. The web terminal is a static web app and is hosted in your web browser and connects to the Altair emulator. When the web terminal connects, the Altair terminal reports the emulator and CP/M versions, and you can start to use the Altair.

The Altair web terminal url is http://aterminal.z8.web.core.windows.net/

Learn more about the Altair emulator web terminal.

To cloud service enable the Altair emulator you must first learn how to Compile and deploy the Altair emulator

For the best experience, use the following cloud services.

  • Open Weather Map provides planet-scale weather and pollution data services. Open Weather Map provides free access to weather and pollution data.
  • Azure IoT Central is a cloud-based Internet of Things (IoT) application platform. You can report, analyze and export IoT data.

docs.title: Cloud service access keys
docs.text: The following pages will show you how to create resources and keys for each service. You'll need to save configuration settings. Copy and paste these settings to a scratch file using a text editor such as Notepad or TextEdit.

docs.title: 01 About IoT Central
docs.text:
Connecting Azure IoT Central is optional and free to try. IoT Central will be very useful as you can stream and report weather, pollution, and diagnostics data, as well as export data for anomaly detection.

In this exercise, you will create an Azure IoT Central application. Later you will learn about Altair applications that stream data to Azure IoT Central. Applications that stream data to Azure IoT Central include WEATHER.BAS and JSON.BAS.

docs.title: Azure IoT Central
docs.text:
Azure IoT Central is a cloud-based Internet of Things (IoT) application platform. It provides an easy way to connect, monitor, and manage your IoT assets at scale. Azure IoT Central builds on Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service, Stream Analytics, and Time Series Insights.

Azure IoT Central follows the eight attributes of successful IoT solutions.

docs.title: Create an Azure IoT Central app
docs.text:
Follow the steps below to create an Azure IoT Central application. You can refer to the Create an IoT Central application guide if you require more information.

  1. Open the Azure IoT Central web portal.

  2. Select Build a solution.

  3. Sign in with your Microsoft personal, work, or school account. If you don't have a Microsoft account, create one for free by using the Create one! link.

  4. Expand the sidebar menu by selecting the Menu icon.

  5. Go to Build, select Custom app, and then select Create app.

  6. Specify the Application name and URL values.

  7. Select the pricing plan. For now, select Free. You can move to a standard plan with two free devices after seven days.

  8. Select Create.

docs.title: 02 IoT Plug and Play
docs.text:
This solution uses IoT Plug and Play with IoT Central. IoT Plug and Play (PnP) defines a model that a device uses to advertise its capabilities to a PnP-enabled application like IoT Central. PnP is an open specification, to learn more, refer to What is IoT Plug and Play.

An IoT Plug and Play CO2 monitor model has been published to the public repository of IoT Plug and Play models. A local copy of the IoT Plug and Play model is located in the iot_plug_and_play directory.

When your device first connects to IoT Central, the IoT Plug and Play model is retrieved from the public repository of models. IoT Central then creates default views using the Plug and Play model.

The IoT Plug and Play model for the CO2 monitor project is declared in main.h.

#define IOT_PLUG_AND_PLAY_MODEL_ID "dtmi:com:example:azuresphere:co2monitor;2"

docs.title: 04 Create an IoT Central app
docs.text:
1. Open the IoT Central web portal by selecting this link Azure IoT Central.

  2. Select Build a solution.

  3. log in with your Microsoft personal, work, or school account. If you don't have a Microsoft account, then you can create one for free by using the Create one! link.

  4. Expand the sidebar menu by selecting the Menu icon.

  5. Navigate to Build, select Custom app, then select Create app.

  6. Specify the Application name and URL.

  7. Select the Free pricing plan. You can migrate to a standard plan with two free devices after seven days.

  8. Select Create.

docs.title: 05 Azure Sphere trust
docs.text:
Once your IoT Central application has been created, you must enable trust between your Azure Sphere tenant and your Azure IoT Central application. Trust is enabled by sharing your Azure Sphere tenant Certificate Authority certificate with your IoT Central application.

When trust is enabled, any device claimed into your trusted Azure Sphere tenant will be enrolled when it first connects to IoT Central.

Follow these steps to enable trust.

  1. Open a command prompt.

  2. Log in to your Azure Sphere tenant. From the command prompt, run:

azsphere login

  1. Make a note of the current folder. You'll need the name of this folder in the next step.

  2. Download the Azure Sphere tenant certificate authority (CA) certificate. From the command prompt, run:

azsphere ca-certificate download --destination CAcertificate.cer

docs.title: Create an Enrollment Group
docs.text:
1. From the IoT Central web portal, select the hamburger button on the top-left corner of the screen to expand the sidebar menu.

  2. Select Administration, then Device Connection.

  3. Select + New.

  4. Name the enrollment group Azure Sphere.

  5. Leave group type set to IoT devices.
  6. Select Certificates (X.509) from the Attestation type dropdown.
  7. Select Save.

docs.title: Upload the Azure Sphere tenant CA certificate to Azure IoT Central
docs.text:
1. Select + Manage primary.

  2. Select the folder icon next to the Primary box and navigate to the folder where you downloaded the certificate. If you don't see the .cer file in the list, set the view filter to **All files () Selecthe certificate and then select the gear icon next to the Primary box.

  3. The Primary Certificate dialog box appears. The Subject and Thumbprint fields contain information about the current Azure Sphere tenant and primary root certificate.

docs.title: Verify the tenant CA certificate
docs.text:
1. Select the Generate verification code.

  2. Copy the verification code to the clipboard.

  3. Download a validation certificate that proves you own the Azure Sphere tenant CA certificate. Replace <code> in the command with the verification code you copied to the clipboard. From a command prompt, run:

azsphere ca-certificate download-proof --destination ValidationCertification.cer --verification-code <code>

The Azure Sphere Security Service signs the validation certificate with the verification code to prove that you own the Certificate Authority (CA).

  1. Return to Azure IoT Central and select Verify.

  2. When prompted, select the validation certificate that you generated in the previous step. When the verification process is complete, the Primary Certificate dialog box displays the Verified message.

  3. Select Close to dismiss the box.

  4. Select Save.

docs.title: 06 IoT Central endpoints
docs.text:
Azure Sphere applications are secure by default, including hardware and network endpoints. You must declare your IoT Central network endpoints, otherwise, your Azure Sphere application will not be able to connect to IoT Central.

Follow these steps to list the network endpoints of your IoT Central application.

  1. Open the Command Prompt window.

  2. Navigate to the azure-sphere-samples folder.

  3. For Windows: Go to the Samples\AzureIoT\Tools\win-x64 folder.

  4. For Linux: Go to the Samples/AzureIoT/Tools/linux-x64 folder# Azure IoT Central.

    You might need to explicitly set execution permissions for the ShowIoTCentralConfig tool. To do so, from a terminal, run chmod +x ShowIoTCentralConfig.

  5. Run the ShowIoTCentralConfig tool, and then follow the prompts, as shown in the following table:

[!NOTE] Your organization might require consent for the ShowIoTCentralConfig tool to access your Azure IoT Central data in the same way that the Azure API requires such consent.

  1. Select Administration > API Tokens > Generate Token.
  2. Provide a name for the token (for example, "AzureSphere").
  3. Select Administrator as the role, and then select Generate.
  4. Copy the token to the clipboard. The token starts with SharedAccessSignature.
ID Scope In the Azure IoT Central application, select Administration > Device Connection, and then copy the ID Scope.
  1. Review the output from the ShowIoTCentralConfig tool. It will look similar to the following JSON text:
"CmdArgs": [ "--ScopeID", "0ne0099999D" ],
"Capabilities": {
   "AllowedConnections": [ "global.azure-devices-provisioning.net", "iotc-9999bc-3305-99ba-885e-6573fc4cf701.azure-devices.net", "iotc-789999fa-8306-4994-b70a-399c46501044.azure-devices.net", "iotc-7a099966-a8c1-4f33-b803-bf29998713787.azure-devices.net", "iotc-97299997-05ab-4988-8142-e299995acdb7.azure-devices.net", "iotc-d099995-7fec-460c-b717-e99999bf4551.azure-devices.net", "iotc-789999dd-3bf5-49d7-9e12-f6999991df8c.azure-devices.net", "iotc-29999917-7344-49e4-9344-5e0cc9999d9b.azure-devices.net", "iotc-99999e59-df2a-41d8-bacd-ebb9999143ab.azure-devices.net", "iotc-c0a9999b-d256-4aaf-aa06-e90e999902b3.azure-devices.net", "iotc-f9199991-ceb1-4f38-9f1c-13199992570e.azure-devices.net" ],
   "DeviceAuthentication": "--- YOUR AZURE SPHERE TENANT ID---",
}
  1. Copy the output from the ShowIoTCentralConfig tool to Notepad, because you'll use this information in a later unit.

docs.title: Add a pollution data visualization view
docs.text:
1. On the left pane, select Views, and then select the Visualizing the device tile.

  2. Name the view pollution.

  3. Select Line chart from the Start with a visual list, then select Add tile.
  4. Select the Size available icon on the tile, and select 4x4.
  5. Select the Edit icon on the tile.
  6. Name the chart Pollution.
  7. Select Past 12 hours from the Display range dropdown list.
  8. Select Capability.
  9. In the capability list, select aqi.
  10. Repeat adding capabilities, and add the following capabilities.
    1. co (carbon monoxide)
    2. nh3 (ammonia)
    3. no (nitrous oxide)
    4. no2 (nitrous dioxide)
    5. o3 (ozone)
    6. pm10 (particulate matter 10)
    7. pm2_5 (particulate matter 2.5)
    8. so2 (sulphur dioxide)
    9. Wind speed

Notes. Pollutants produced by vehicle exhausts include carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides, particles, volatile organic compounds, and sulfur dioxide. Hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides react with sunlight and warm temperatures to form ground-level ozone. Ground-level ozone, a key ingredient in smog, can cause upper respiratory problems and lung damage.

docs.title: Open Weather Map
docs.text: Connecting the Open Weather Map cloud service is optional, free, and recommended so the Altair emulator can stream weather and pollution information to Azure IoT Central.

docs.title: Create an Open Weather Map API Key
docs.text:
1. From your web browser navigate to https://openweathermap.org/api
  2. Sign in to Open Weather Map
  3. Select API from the Open Weather Map main menu.
  4. Subscribe to the Current Weather Data. Select the Free option, and select Get API key.
  5. Repeat and subscribe to the Air Pollution API. Select the Free option, and select Get API key.

docs.title: Open Weather Map air quality calculation
docs.text:
Open Weather Map air quality calculation is based on the Common Air Quality Index (CAQI). The Common Air Quality Index (CAQI) is an air quality index used in Europe since 2006.

For more information, refer to the calculation of Air Quality index.

docs.title: Open Weather Map weather and pollution service
docs.text:
To connect the Altair emulator to the Open Weather Map weather and pollution APIs you'll need to declare the Open Weather Map API key.

"CmdArgs": [
    "--ScopeID",
    "",
    "-o",
    "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_OPEN_WEATHER_MAP_API_KEY"
],

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. If you have trouble connecting to the Azure Sphere over USB be sure to disable any VPNs you might have enabled.
  2. The TAP-Windows Adapter V9 installed with VPN clients, including the OpenVPN client is not compatible with the TAP-Windows Adapter V9 required and installed by the Azure Sphere SDK. You will need to uninstall the VPN client and reinstall the Azure Sphere SDK for Visual Studio.
  3. Windows Users. If running the IoT Central ShowIoTCentralConfig command fails with a missing library message then delete the folder from ShowIoTCentralConfig from AppData\Local\Temp\.net.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Follow the Windows or Ubuntu Quickstarts linked below to install the developer tools required to build and deploy the Predictive Maintenance.

docs.title: Windows users
docs.text:
Azure Sphere development is supported on Windows 10 and 11.

You need to complete these steps:

  1. Install the latest Azure Sphere SDK.
  2. Install CMake and Ninja.
  3. Install Visual Studio Code.
  4. Install the Visual Studio Code Azure Sphere extension.
  5. Claim your device.
  6. Configure networking for the device.

The Quickstart: Install the Azure Sphere SDK for Windows will step you through the process.

docs.title: Install the Git client for Windows
docs.text:
The Git client is required to clone the Predictive Maintenance solution to your computer.

Install Git for Windows.

docs.title: Install the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain for Windows
docs.text:
1. Download the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain for Windows.
  2. Install the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain

docs.title: Ubuntu users
docs.text:
Azure Sphere development is supported on Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 LTS.

You need to do the following:

  1. Install the Azure Sphere SDK.
  2. Set up the device connection.
  3. Install CMake and Ninja.
  4. Install Visual Studio Code.
  5. Install the Visual Studio Code Azure Sphere extension.
  6. Claim your device.
  7. Configure networking for the device.

The Quickstart: Install the Azure Sphere SDK for Linux will step you through the process.

docs.title: Install the Git client for Linux
docs.text:
The Git client is required to clone the Predictive Maintenance solution to your computer.

sudo apt install git

docs.title: Install the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain for Linux
docs.text:
Install the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain for Linux

  1. Download the latest GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain.

  2. Install the downloaded package. The following command installs the toolchain in the /opt directory. Note, you will need to update the filename to match the version you downloaded.

    sudo tar -xjvf gcc-arm-none-eabi-10.3-2021.10-x86_64-linux.tar.bz2 -C /opt

  3. Update your path. Open ~/.bashrc and add to the end.

    export PATH=$PATH:/opt/gcc-arm-none-eabi-10.3-2021.10/bin

  4. Optional: The real-time core debugger relies on the libncurses.so.5 library. Depending on your system setup, this library may already be install, if not, then run the following commands.

    sudo add-apt-repository universe
sudo apt-get install libncurses5

docs.title: Recommended Visual Studio Code Extension
docs.text:
The Peacock extension allows you to change the color of your Visual Studio Code workspace. The Peacock extension is useful when you have multiple instances of Visual Studio Code open debugging code on high-level and real-time cores.

  1. Open Extensions sideBar panel in Visual Studio Code
    • Or choose the menu options for View → Extensions
  2. Search for Peacock
  3. Click Install
  4. Click Reload, if required

docs.title: Delete existing applications on Azure Sphere
docs.text:
1. From the Windows PowerShell command-line or Linux Terminal, run the following command to delete any existing applications on the device.
azsphere device sideload delete
  1. Restart Azure Sphere.
azsphere device restart

docs.title: Enable high-level core development
docs.text:
1. From the Windows PowerShell command-line or Linux Terminal, run the following command to enable high-level app development on the device.
azsphere device enable-development

docs.title: Windows users
docs.text:
1. Open the Windows PowerShell command-line as Administrator, and run the following command to enable real-time core development on the device.
azsphere device enable-development -r
  1. Close the Windows PowerShell command-line

docs.text:

Learning how to program the Altair 8800 emulator is a great way to learn about the history of computing and the fundamentals of computer programming.

docs.title: Editing Files: Developer Workflow
docs.text:
You can work with files for the Altair CP/M system in two primary ways:

  1. External editor on your host (Recommended) – Edit locally with a modern editor such as Visual Studio Code. This gives you syntax highlighting, search, Copilot / LLM assistance, version control, etc.
  2. On‑emulator editing (Word-Master) – Edit inside the emulated CP/M environment using the bundled Word-Master editor. Authentic, but slower and less ergonomic for substantial changes.

docs.title: Editing Files with External Tools (Recommended)
docs.text:
Follow this fast loop for most development:

  1. Pick an editor – Example: Visual Studio Code (with optional Copilot / LLM assistance).
  2. Create a folder on your host computer to hold your source files.
  3. Create or modify your source – Edit as normal on your host (BASIC, C, ASM, etc.).
  4. Build C on the host using dcc and the app's build-app.ps1, or use dccmake for a build without installing into a disk image. See C Programming.
  5. Make text/assembly files available to FT. ESP32 uses its configured remote FT server. The retired GF HTTP utility and BDS build workflows are not supported.

  6. Transfer a file into CP/M with the current FT client:

    ft -g games/awari.bas

    (File names are case‑insensitive; CP/M convention is uppercase.)

  7. Run or build – Examples:

    • BASIC: mbasic awari.

Repeat the edit/build/transfer steps as you refine your program. FT -g normalizes text to CP/M line endings; use -gb for a prebuilt .COM file. FT is not an arbitrary HTTP/GitHub downloader.

docs.text:

docs.title: ROMless service I/O reference
docs.text: ESP32 and the Altair DCC debug adapter compile the same io_ports.c transport. Platform drivers supply the service backends. The local SBC emulator and Apple container use the SBC adapter and its I/O port map.

docs.title: Address decoding and allocation
docs.text:
The service router decodes address & 0x17, giving 16 canonical addresses. Use canonical addresses in programs. The physical ROMless allocation reserves terminal, disk and diagnostic addresses:

Hex Decimal Physical ROMless allocation 0x00 0 Terminal data 0x01 1 Terminal status 0x02 2 Shared service command (OUT) / status (IN) 0x03 3 Shared length-prefixed request (OUT) 0x04 4 Shared length-prefixed response (IN) 0x05 5 Reserved BIOS/qualification diagnostics 0x06 6 Reserved diagnostic data 0x07 7 Interrupt timer rate (OUT/IN) 0x10 16 Disk command/status 0x11 17 Disk drive selection 0x12 18 Disk sector address low 0x13 19 Disk sector address high 0x14 20 Disk data 0x15 21 Available 0x16 22 Available 0x17 23 Dedicated countdown/stopwatch interface

docs.title: Emulator versus physical hardware
docs.text: The emulator's CPU adapter intercepts terminal ports 0x00/0x01 and 0x10/0x11, disk ports 0x08/0x09/0x0A, and front-panel input 0xFF before forwarding other ports to the service router. These intercepts support the supplied CP/M disks. Do not apply & 0x17 globally: that would alias emulator disk ports onto terminal/service ports.

docs.title: Shared transport conventions
docs.text:
Command bytes identify groups, not physical ports. Group requests begin with an operation byte. All u16/u32 values use little-endian wire order. The CP/M SDK reference describes the C helpers.

Command Group 0x00 ACK: acknowledge COMPLETE or a fully consumed error 0x01 RESET: abandon/reset the shared transport 0x02 IDENTIFY: return ROMLESS-SVC/1 0x10 Countdown timers 0x11 Stopwatches 0x20 Clock/date/uptime 0x21 Utilities/system information/reboot 0x30 Persistent environment variables and CLI 0x40 Weather 0x50 Chat 0x60 Host Sense HAT panel/sensors 0x70 File transfer

docs.title: Framing and status
docs.text:
1. Wait for READY on IN 0x02.
  2. Write the group to OUT 0x02.
  3. Write a u16 payload length to OUT 0x03, then exactly that many payload bytes. Execution starts after the final byte.
  4. Poll IN 0x02 with a bounded timeout.
  5. On RESPONSE_READY, read a u16 length from IN 0x04, then that many response bytes. Consuming the full frame returns READY.
  6. On COMPLETE, write ACK to OUT 0x02.
  7. On ERROR, consume its framed error code and ACK, or RESET.

ACK, RESET and IDENTIFY execute immediately without request framing. IDENTIFY requires READY and returns a normal framed response.

Status Meaning 0x00 READY 0x01 COMPLETE; ACK required 0x02 RESPONSE_READY 0x03 COLLECTING request length/payload 0x04 BUSY 0xFF ERROR; framed error available

Status polling neither acknowledges completion nor consumes payload. Text excludes its terminating NUL; binary zero is ordinary data. The shared payload limit is 2048 bytes, excluding the two length bytes. Do not truncate a request or response and report success.

Only one shared transaction may be active. A group command during an active transaction produces a busy/state error and requires RESET. ACK is valid only for COMPLETE or a fully consumed error. RESET discards partial frames and invalidates late worker completions. A worker-backed request can remain BUSY while an abandoned job finishes.

Common error codes are 0x01 unknown group, 0x02 unknown operation, 0x03 invalid length, 0x04 invalid parameter, 0x05 unavailable, 0x06 busy, 0x07 timeout, 0x08 invalid state, 0x09 response underflow, 0x10 storage open, 0x11 storage read, 0x12 storage write, 0x13 capacity, 0x14 not found, 0x15 unsynchronized clock, 0x16 invalid reboot confirmation, 0x20 missing HTTP base URL, and 0x21 transfer failure. Error codes are not port addresses.

docs.title: Execution ownership
docs.text:
Calendar, environment, weather, chat and utility transactions use a worker: Core 0 on ESP32, a background thread on hosts. The CPU polls completion without blocking on network or flash operations. Timer groups are synchronous CPU-thread operations sharing state with port 0x17.

FT has its own backend. ESP32 uses queued Core 0 TCP work; the DCC adapter reads the configured filesystem. FT reads occupy the shared transaction until their response is consumed. Between reads, other shared services can run without closing the FT session. Interrupt rate and dedicated timer operations remain independent of shared transactions.

io_ports_init() starts the shared worker after platform initialization; shutdown stops it and closes FT. Response generation tags prevent abandoned jobs from replacing a current response. ESP32 FT queue replies own their payload until the CPU consumes them.

docs.title: Dedicated timer port: 0x17 (decimal 23)
docs.text:
All countdown and stopwatch commands, parameters and results use port 23, without framing, BUSY polling or ACK.

OUT command Following OUT bytes IN result 0x00 None Reset interface; countdown running mask 0x10-0x12 Duration u16 Start millisecond timer 0-2; running mask 0x13 Duration u8 Start seconds timer 3; running mask 0x20-0x23 None Selected countdown: 1 running, 0 expired/unset 0x30 None Running mask, bits 0-3 0x40-0x42 None Reset stopwatch 0-2; running mask 0x50-0x52 None Stopwatch seconds, u32 0x60-0x62 None Stopwatch milliseconds, u32

Timers 0-2 accept 0-65535 ms; timer 3 accepts 0-255 seconds. Zero expires immediately. A complete duration replaces its timer atomically. Stopwatch reads latch all four bytes at command time; values wrap modulo 2^32. Before first reset, stopwatches measure time since boot.

Finish parameter writes and drain all four stopwatch bytes before another user accesses this interface. Invalid commands, interrupted parameters and response overreads enter an error state (IN returns 0xFF). Recover with one IN 23, then OUT 23,0; this does not change timers or the shared channel. 0xFF within a valid stopwatch response is ordinary data.

The SDK timer helpers use this interface. Groups 0x10/0x11 provide framed access to the same timers/stopwatches with separate transaction state.

docs.title: Countdown timers and stopwatches: 0x10/0x11
docs.text: Countdown START is [0, id, duration:u32], returning COMPLETE; QUERY is [1, id], returning one running byte. IDs and ranges match port 0x17. Stopwatch requests are [operation, id]: 0 reset (COMPLETE), 1 read seconds (u32), 2 read milliseconds (u32). IDs are 0-2.

docs.title: Clock and utilities: 0x20/0x21
docs.text:
Clock requests contain one operation byte: 0 boot seconds, 1 UTC ISO time, 2 local ISO time, 3 long local date, 4 DATE-style local time. Results are text. Calendar requests fail explicitly when the clock is unsynchronized.

Utility requests are [0] for two random bytes; [1, selector] for hostname (0), IP (1), or device ID (2); [2, 0xA5] for confirmed reboot; and [3] for firmware version text. ESP32 schedules reboot outside the CPU handler after COMPLETE. Host builds report UNAVAILABLE for reboot.

docs.title: Environment: 0x30
docs.text:
Keys, values and CLI lines are raw text without a terminating NUL.

Request payload Successful result [0] RESET COMPLETE; clear ENV request state [1] INIT COMPLETE [2, key_length, key...] GET Value text [3, key_length, key..., value_length:u16, value...] SET COMPLETE [4, key_length, key...] DELETE COMPLETE [5] LIST Formatted key/value text [6] COUNT Decimal entry count text [7] CLEAR COMPLETE [8, key_length, key...] EXISTS COMPLETE if present; NOT_FOUND otherwise [9, line...] EXECUTE CLI result text, possibly empty

Requests are self-contained and reject embedded NULs and inconsistent lengths. Keys are normalized and limited to 16 characters, values to 255, and CLI lines to 511. LIST overflow is an explicit capacity error. Empty values are valid; missing keys return NOT_FOUND.

docs.title: Weather: 0x40
docs.text:
[0, field] returns field text; [1] returns weather-service status: 0 no data, 1 fetching, 2 ready, 3 error. This payload byte is independent of shared transaction status.

Fields are 0 city, 1 current main, 2 current description, 3 temperature, 4 humidity, 5 wind, 6 forecast main, 7 forecast description, 8 forecast temperature, 9 forecast valid-at time, 10 last-fetch age (seconds), 11 units, 12 last error, 13 current feels-like temperature, 14 forecast feels-like temperature.

Cached readings remain available during refresh or a subsequent fetch error. Missing readings report UNAVAILABLE. Units/error diagnostics are readable without cached measurements.

docs.title: Chat: 0x50
docs.text:
Request payload Successful result [0] RESET_REQUEST COMPLETE; empty the assembled request [1, text bytes...] APPEND COMPLETE [2] RESET_RESPONSE COMPLETE [3] SUBMIT COMPLETE once queued [4] STATUS Stream-status byte: 0 EOF, 1 waiting, 2 data ready [5, maximum:u16] READ_CHUNK [stream_status, count:u16, bytes...]

APPEND accepts up to 2047 text bytes per transaction within the backend's request capacity, reserving room for its internal NUL. SUBMIT resets response generation but preserves the assembled request. Reject a second SUBMIT while a chat job is active. Completion is queue acceptance, not network completion.

READ_CHUNK accepts a maximum of 1-256 and does not wait for network data. Available bytes have status 2 and a positive count; waiting/EOF have zero count and status 1/0. Deliver buffered bytes before EOF. Each chunk is a separate transaction, allowing other services between reads. ESP32 applies queue back-pressure; host ring overflow has an explicit truncation marker. An unavailable backend reports an error, not EOF-shaped success.

docs.title: Sense HAT: 0x60
docs.text: Requests are [selector, data]: selectors 63 sensor read, 65 panel color, 80 mode, 81 font color, 85 character, 90-97 bitmap rows, 98 pixel on, 99 pixel off, 100 pixel flip, 101 clear, 102 draw. These are operation bytes, not ports. Sensor selection uses data and returns text; panel writes return COMPLETE. Unsupported/absent hardware returns UNAVAILABLE, including on ESP32 and the DCC adapter.

docs.title: File transfer: 0x70
docs.text:
Request payload Successful result [1, filename bytes...] Open/replace session; COMPLETE, then ACK [3] [state, up to 256 file bytes...] [4] Cancel/close; COMPLETE, then ACK

Filenames contain 1-127 bytes without a terminating NUL. Read and close accept no extra bytes. State 0 means more data; 2 means EOF, optionally with final bytes. Empty EOF has payload [2] and length 1; a full chunk has length 257. Consume the entire framed response before another request. Repeated EOF reads return empty EOF. Transfer failures return error 0x21. RESET during a BUSY read cancels the FT session; close also invalidates pending replies and buffered data. Other service transactions between FT reads preserve its filename and offset.

ESP32 connects to its configured remote FT server on TCP port 8090. The DCC adapter uses the session's native files root. This shared ABI also supports HTTP(S) hosts: error 0x20 means their required HTTP_BASE_URL is missing.

docs.title: Interrupt timer: physical port 0x07
docs.text: OUT 0x07 sets 0 to disable or 1-255 Hz and clears pending timer requests. IN 0x07 returns the configured rate, not an interrupt-pending flag. The emulator's interrupt provider/acknowledgement path is independent of shared transactions. A physical implementation requires an INT/acknowledge path; a port assignment alone does not provide interrupt wiring.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
cmake -S dcc_debug_io_adapter -B dcc_debug_io_adapter/build
cmake --build dcc_debug_io_adapter/build
ctest --test-dir dcc_debug_io_adapter/build --output-on-failure

The adapter tests cover service framing, invalid requests, ACK/RESET, abandoned replies and error recovery.

docs.title: What is Vibe-Engineering with an LLM?
docs.text: Vibe engineering is a programming approach that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in writing code. It involves using AI tools to generate, complete, or suggest code snippets based on natural language prompts or partial code inputs. This method can significantly speed up the coding process, help overcome writer's block, and provide creative solutions to programming challenges.

docs.title: Why Use Vibe-Engineering for the Altair 8800?
docs.text:
The Altair 8800 is a vintage microcomputer that has a unique architecture and programming environment. Vibe-Engineering can help modern developers interact with this classic system by:

  • Generating code snippets compatible with the Altair's architecture.
  • Providing explanations and documentation for legacy programming concepts.
  • Assisting in debugging and optimizing code for the Altair.

docs.title: Getting Started with Vibe-Engineering for the Altair 8800
docs.text:
1. Choose an LLM Tool: Select a Large Language Model platform that supports code generation, such as OpenAI's Codex, Claude Opus or similar services.
  2. Set Up Your Environment: Ensure you have access to the Altair 8800 emulator or hardware, along with any necessary development tools.
  3. Define Your Goals: Clearly outline what you want to achieve with your Altair programming project.
  4. Craft Prompts: Write clear and specific prompts to guide the LLM in generating relevant code snippets.
  5. Iterate and Refine: Use the generated code as a starting point, test it on the Altair, and refine it as needed.

docs.title: Shared service client
docs.text: Current dcc applications share Apps/COMMON/DXSVC.C and its header. Use the service ABI and C programming guide when generating new code.

docs.title: Leverage existing code samples
docs.text:
Point the LLM to current Apps sources and their dcc build configurations:

  • COMMON/DXSVC.C
  • BREAKOUT/breakc11.c
  • TETRIS/tetris_c11.c
  • CLOCK/CLOCK.C

Are great examples how to use the IO ports and other features such as timers and VT100 terminal control characters of the Altair 8800 for Vibe-Engineering.

For an Intel 8080 assembly example, see VIBE.ASM. It uses countdown timer 2 on dedicated port 23: write command 0x12, then the 50 ms duration as low/high bytes (50, 0), and select status with 0x22. Repeated reads return 1 while running and 0 on expiry. The old timer ports 28-29 are no longer supported; see the timer ABI.

When crafting prompts for the LLM, consider including references to existing documentation and manuals for the Altair 8800. This can help the model generate more accurate and contextually relevant code. Useful resources include:

docs.title: Example Prompts for Vibe-Engineering
docs.text:
• "Write a BASIC program for the Altair 8800 that calculates the factorial of a number."
  • "Explain how to set up I/O ports on the Altair 8800."

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Review Generated Code: Always review and test the code generated by the LLM to ensure it meets your requirements and is free of errors.
  • Combine with Traditional Coding: Use Vibe-Engineering as a supplement to your traditional coding practices.
  • Stay Updated: Keep abreast of advancements in LLM technology to leverage new features and capabilities.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Vibe-Engineering with an LLM can be a powerful tool for programming the Altair 8800, making it easier to navigate its unique challenges and unlock its potential. By integrating AI into your development workflow, you can enhance productivity and creativity in your projects.

docs.title: Intel 8080 IO Ports
docs.text: The Intel 8080 can address 256 input ports and 256 output ports. Programs access them with the IN and OUT instructions. This page documents the current port assignments used by the Altair emulator.

docs.title: Port assignments
docs.text:
The emulator decodes the port address with address & 0x17. Use the canonical addresses in this table in programs and documentation.

Address Decimal Direction Purpose 0x02 2 IN / OUT Shared-service status and command 0x03 3 OUT Shared-service request length and payload 0x04 4 IN Shared-service response length and payload 0x07 7 IN / OUT Interrupt timer rate 0x15 21 - Available 0x16 22 - Available 0x17 23 IN / OUT Countdown timers and stopwatches

Terminal and disk ports are handled by the emulator's existing console and disk interfaces.

docs.title: Shared services on ports 0x02-0x04
docs.text:
Write a service group to OUT 0x02, then write a two-byte payload length to OUT 0x03 (low byte first), followed by exactly that many payload bytes. The first payload byte is the operation. Poll IN 0x02 until the request finishes. For a response, read its two-byte length from IN 0x04 (low byte first), then read exactly that many bytes. A response is binary-safe: zero is ordinary data and text responses do not include a trailing NUL. For a command with no response, acknowledge COMPLETE by writing 0x00 to OUT 0x02. On ERROR, read the complete error frame and acknowledge it; write RESET (0x01) to OUT 0x02 to abandon a partial request or recover an unknown state.

Group byte Service 0x10 Countdown timers 0x11 Stopwatches 0x20 Clock, date and uptime 0x21 Random numbers, system information and reboot 0x30 Environment variables and CLI commands 0x40 Weather 0x50 Chat 0x60 Sense HAT on supported host builds 0x70 File transfer

Status values from IN 0x02 are 0x00 READY, 0x01 COMPLETE, 0x02 RESPONSE_READY, 0x03 COLLECTING, 0x04 BUSY and 0xFF ERROR. A framed error response contains an error code as its first payload byte. The shared payload limit is 2048 bytes. Only one shared transaction may be active at a time. Poll with a bounded timeout. See the dcc client API for C helpers and service operation details.

docs.title: dcc C example
docs.text:
The shared dcc client provides typed functions for common operations. This example starts a 100 ms timer and waits for it to expire:

#include "DXSVC.H"

int main(void)
{
    svc_start_timer(1, 100);
    while (svc_timer_active(1))
        ;
    return 0;
}

The same client provides svc_random_u16() and svc_access_stopwatch(). Use svc_call_service() or svc_operation_send() for other framed requests.

docs.title: Countdown timers and stopwatches on 0x17
docs.text:
All timer operations use OUT 0x17 for a command and its parameters, and IN 0x17 for results. This dedicated interface does not use shared-service framing or acknowledgements.

OUT command Following OUT bytes IN result 0x00 None Reset interface; return to running-mask mode 0x10-0x12 Duration u16, little-endian Start millisecond timer 0-2 0x13 Duration u8 Start seconds timer 3 0x20-0x23 None Select timer 0-3; read 1 while running, 0 when expired 0x30 None Read running mask; bits 0-3 represent timers 0-3 0x40-0x42 None Reset stopwatch 0-2 0x50-0x52 None Read stopwatch seconds as four little-endian bytes 0x60-0x62 None Read stopwatch milliseconds as four little-endian bytes

Timer IDs 0-2 accept durations from 0 to 65535 milliseconds. Timer 3 accepts 0 to 255 seconds. A zero duration expires immediately. Stopwatch results are unsigned 32-bit values; read all four bytes after selecting a stopwatch.

Example 8080 assembly starts timer 1 for 100 ms and polls it:

        MVI A,11H      ; select timer 1 start
        OUT 23
        MVI A,64H      ; duration low byte: 100 ms
        OUT 23
        MVI A,00H      ; duration high byte
        OUT 23
        MVI A,21H      ; select timer 1 query
        OUT 23
WAIT:   IN 23
        CPI 01H
        JZ WAIT

Finish a multi-byte command or read all four stopwatch bytes before another port-0x17 user accesses the interface. To recover an unknown parser state, read 0x17 once and then write 0x00 to it. This resets the interface without changing running timers or stopwatch values.

docs.title: Interrupt timer on 0x07
docs.text:
• OUT 0x07: set the interrupt rate in hertz; zero disables it.
  • IN 0x07: read the configured rate.

This port reports the rate, not a pending-interrupt flag.

docs.title: File transfer: shared group 0x70
docs.text:
The FT CP/M application uses the shared framing on ports 0x02/0x03/0x04. Filename requests contain 1-127 bytes without a terminating NUL.

Request payload Result [1, filename bytes...] Open/replace session; COMPLETE, then ACK [3] RESPONSE_READY: [state, up to 256 file bytes...] [4] Cancel/close; COMPLETE, then ACK

State 0 means more data; 2 means EOF and may accompany final bytes. An empty EOF response is [2] with framed length 1; a full chunk has length 257. File bytes, including zero, are ordinary payload. Fully consuming a response returns READY. Other shared services can run between reads without closing the FT session. RESET while a read is BUSY cancels that session. Transfer failure returns shared error 0x21.

ESP32 uses its remote FT TCP server on port 8090. See the complete service reference for transport recovery and backend details.

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text: The ENV CP/M application provides a reboot menu option with user confirmation. Reboot requests use utility group 0x21, operation 0x02, and confirmation byte 0xA5, sent through the shared-service protocol.

docs.title: Microsoft BASIC
docs.text:
Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote Altair BASIC. It was Microsoft's first product. Later, Microsoft released Microsoft BASIC for CP/M, see the Microsoft BASIC-80 reference manual.

In the following exercise, you'll learn how to write your first Microsoft BASIC application.

docs.title: Get started with Microsoft BASIC-80
docs.text:
Microsoft BASIC-80 is included on drive A.

  1. Switch back to the web terminal in your web browser.

  2. From the CP/M command prompt, run the following command to start Microsoft BASIC.

    mbasic

  3. Run an interactive command

    print "Hello, world!"

    The BASIC interpreter with execute the command immediately and display Hello, World!.

  4. Enter your first program:

    10 for i = 1 to 1000000
20 print i
30 next i

  5. Run your program

    run

  6. Stop the program by selecting Ctrl+C.

  7. Save your program to disk:

    save "TEST.BAS"

    Name all files using CAPITAL LETTERS.

  8. Load your program from disk:

    load "TEST.BAS"

  9. Quit BASIC:

    system

  10. Run the following command to start your BASIC application from the CP/M command prompt.

    mbasic test

You can learn more about BASIC from the following BASIC applications included with the Altair emulator:

  • COUNT.BAS demonstrates how to use the Intel 8080 IO Port 30 to sleep or delay an application for a specific period.
  • DISKRW.BAS is a test application that opens and repeatedly reads and writes a text file.
  • FONT.BAS shows how to write ASCII characters to the 8x8 LED panels on the Pi Sense HAT or Retro Click.
  • JSON.BAS reads weather and pollution data and then publishes JSON data to Azure IoT Central.
  • LOOPY.BAS is a test application that generates a lot of messages.
  • STARTREK.BAS is a game.
  • TICTAK.BAS: A simple game of naughts and crosses.
  • TIME.BAS demonstrates how to use the time Intel 8080 IO ports including setting a sleep timer, access to the system tick counter, and local and UTC date and times.
  • WEATHER.BAS reads weather and pollution data from Open Weather Map and adds random jitter to the temperature data at random intervals. The jittered temperature is used for anomaly detection. The weather and pollution data is then streamed to Azure IoT Central at regular intervals.

docs.title: Use Intel 8080 input and output ports
docs.text:
The BASIC language has support for Intel 8080 CPU input and output port instructions. The TIME.BAS application:

  • gets the system tick count from port 41
  • gets the UTC date and time from port 42
  • gets the local date and time from port 43
  • and sets a sleep period using output port 30, and then waits on input port 30 for the delay period to expire.

For more information about Intel 8080 IO port mappings, refer to Intel 8080 input and output ports.

The following BASIC program is the listing of TIME.BAS. The Time app uses color escape codes to control text colors.

10 WIDTH 100
20 PRINT "===================================================="
30 PRINT "TIME DEMOS"
40 SECONDS% = 1

50 WHILE 1
60 PRINT "==============================================="

70 PORT = 41 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[91;22;24m" + "System tick count: ";RSTRING$;chr$(27) + "[0m"
80 PORT = 42 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[92;22;24m" + "UTC date and time: ";RSTRING;chr$(27) + "[0m"
90 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[94;22;24m" + "Local date and time: ";RSTRING$; chr$(27) + "[0m"

130 GOSUB 230

140 WEND
150 END

160 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
170 RSTRING$ = ""
175 OUT PORT, 0
180 C=INP(200)
190 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
200 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
210 GOTO 180

220 REM PAUSE FOR N NUMBER OF SECONDS
230 PRINT "" : PRINT "Pause";SECONDS%;"seconds."
240 OUT 30, SECONDS%
250 WAIT 30, 1, 1
260 RETURN

docs.title: Run the TIME.BAS application
docs.text:
1. To start Microsoft BASIC, from the CP/M command prompt, enter:

    mbasic time

    Microsoft BASIC starts and runs the TIME.BAS application. The TIME.BAS application displays the system tick count, along with the local and UTC date and time.

  2. Stop the program by selecting Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Run the WEATHER.BAS application
docs.text:
The WEATHER.BAS application reads weather and pollution data provided by Open Weather Map. Like the COUNT.BAS application, WEATHER.BAS uses Intel 8080 IO Ports to access the data.

The following BASIC program is the listing of WEATHER.BAS:

200 PRINT "===================================================="
300 PRINT "OPEN WEATHER MAP IOT APP"
400 SECONDS% = 10
500 WEATHERKEY = 34
600 WEATHERVALUE = 35
700 WEATHERITEMS = 6
800 LOCATIONKEY = 36
900 LOCATIONVALUE = 37
1000 LOCATIONITEMS = 4
1100 POLLUTIONKEY = 38
1200 POLLUTIONVALUE = 39
1300 POLLUTIONITEMS = 9
1400 PRINT "PUBLISH WEATHER DATA TO IOT CENTRAL EVERY";SECONDS%;"SECONDS"
1500 RCOUNT% = 0
1600 READING# = 0
1700 WHILE 1
1800 READING# = READING# + 1
1900 PRINT "============================================================================================================================"
2000 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 4300 : TIME$ = RSTRING$
2100 PRINT "Reading", "Time"
2200 PRINT READING#,  TIME$
2300 ITEMKEY = WEATHERKEY : ITEMVALUE = WEATHERVALUE : ITEMS = WEATHERITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2400 PRINT
2500 ITEMKEY = POLLUTIONKEY : ITEMVALUE = POLLUTIONVALUE : ITEMS = POLLUTIONITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2600 PRINT
2700 ITEMKEY = LOCATIONKEY : ITEMVALUE = LOCATIONVALUE : ITEMS = LOCATIONITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2800 PRINT
2900 GOSUB 5400 : REM PUBLISH WEATHER DATA
3000 GOSUB 5000 : REM SLEEP
3100 WEND
3200 END
3300 REM PRINT ITEM KEY VALUE PAIRS
3400 PRINT
3500 FOR I = 1 TO ITEMS
3600 PORT = ITEMKEY : PDATA = I - 1 : GOSUB 4300 : PRINT RSTRING$, 
3700 NEXT I
3800 PRINT
3900 FOR I = 1 TO ITEMS
4000 PORT = ITEMVALUE : PDATA = I - 1 : GOSUB 4300 : PRINT RSTRING$, 
4100 NEXT I
4200 RETURN
4300 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
4400 OUT PORT, PDATA
4500 RSTRING$ = ""
4600 C=INP(200)
4700 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
4800 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
4900 GOTO 4600
5000 PRINT "" : PRINT CHR$(27) + "[31;22;24m" + "Sleep for"; SECONDS% ; "seconds." + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
5100 OUT 30, SECONDS%
5200 IF INP(30) = 1 THEN GOTO 5200
5300 RETURN
5400 REM PUBLISH WEATHER DATA
5500 REM WAIT FOR PUBLISH WEATHER PENDING TO GO FALSE
5600 WAIT 32, 1, 1
5700 REM PUBLISH TO IOT CENTRAL WITH JITTER
5800 OUT 32, 0
5900 RETURN

When you run this application, weather and pollution data are published to Azure IoT Central. You can view the data in the Azure IoT Central web portal, from the Pollution and Weather tabs for your device.

docs.title: Generating anomaly weather data
docs.text:
The anomaly app publishes weather data sourced from Open Weather Map to Azure IoT Central. The anomaly app adds random jitter values to the temperature. The jitter values are added to the temperature so you can see the effect of anomalies when using the Azure Anomaly Detection Cognitive Service.

100 WIDTH 150
200 PRINT "===================================================="
300 PRINT "OPEN WEATHER MAP IOT APP"
400 DELAY% = 10
500 WEATHERPORT = 35
600 LOCATIONPORT = 37
700 POLLUTIONPORT = 39
800 DEF FNNEXTJITTER(ROW#, DELAY%) = ROW# + 1 + (INT(RND * 60) * 180 / DELAY% )
900 DEF FNJITTERTEMPERATURE(TEMPERATURE$) = VAL(TEMPERATURE$) + 30 - INT(RND * 20) : REM Return temperature plus random value
1000 REM GET RANDOM NUMBER SEED FROM PLATFORM
1100 PORT = 44 : GOSUB 4700 : RANDOMIZE VAL(RSTRING$)
1200 PRINT "SEND WEATHER DATA TO IOT CENTRAL EVERY";DELAY%;"SECONDS"
1300 RCOUNT# = 0
1400 NEXTJITTER# = FNNEXTJITTER(RCOUNT#, DELAY%)
1500 WHILE 1
1600 RCOUNT# = RCOUNT# + 1
1700 PRINT "===================================================="
1800 PRINT CHR$(27) + "[33;22;24m" + "Reading:"; RCOUNT#; "| Next jitter:";NEXTJITTER#; "| BASIC free memory:"; FRE(0); CHR$(27) + "[0m"
1900 REM GET TIME AS STRING
2000 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 4700 : PRINT "Time (local): ";RSTRING$
2100 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : TEMPERATURE$ = RSTRING$
2200 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 1 : GOSUB 4700 : PRESSURE$ = RSTRING$
2300 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 2 : GOSUB 4700 : HUMIDITY$ = RSTRING$
2400 PORT = POLLUTIONPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : AIRQUALITYINDEX$ = RSTRING$
2500 PORT = LOCATIONPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : LATITUDE$ = RSTRING$
2600 PORT = LOCATIONPORT : PDATA = 1 : GOSUB 4700 : LONGITUDE$ = RSTRING$
2700 IF RCOUNT# = NEXTJITTER# THEN TEMPERATURE$ = STR$(FNJITTERTEMPERATURE(TEMPERATURE$)) : NEXTJITTER# = FNNEXTJITTER(RCOUNT#, DELAY%)
2800 PRINT : PRINT "Celsius", "Millibars", "Humidity %", "AQI (CAQI)", "Latitude", "Longitude"
2900 PRINT TEMPERATURE$, PRESSURE$, HUMIDITY$, AIRQUALITYINDEX$, LATITUDE$, LONGITUDE$
3000 PRINT
3100 GOSUB 3700 : REM Generate JSON
3200 GOSUB 5900 : REM Publish JSON
3300 PRINT: PRINT CHR$(27) + "[31;22;24m" + "Sleep for";DELAY%;"seconds." + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
3400 GOSUB 5400
3500 WEND
3600 END
3700 REM BUILD JSON STRING
3800 RJSON$ = "{"
3900 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "temperature" + CHR$(34) + ":" + TEMPERATURE$ + ","
4000 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "pressure" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  PRESSURE$ + ","
4100 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "humidity" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  HUMIDITY$ + ","
4200 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "latitude" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  LATITUDE$ + ","
4300 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "longitude" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  LONGITUDE$ + ","
4400 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "aqi" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  AIRQUALITYINDEX$
4500 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + "}"
4600 RETURN
4700 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
4800 OUT PORT, PDATA
4900 RSTRING$ = ""
5000 C=INP(200)
5100 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
5200 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
5300 GOTO 5000
5400 REM SUBROUTINE DELAYS PROGRAM EXECUTION BY DELAY% SECONDS
5500 OUT 30, DELAY%
5600 IF INP(30) = 1 THEN GOTO 5600
5700 WAIT 31, 1, 1 : REM WAIT FOR PUBLISH JSON PENDING TO GO FALSE
5800 RETURN
5900 REM SUBROUTINE PUBLISHES JSON TO AZURE IOT
6000 LENGTH% = LEN(RJSON$)
6100 IF LENGTH% = 0 THEN RETURN
6200 IF LENGTH% > 256 THEN RETURN
6300 PRINT CHR$(27) + "[94;22;24m" + "PUBLISHING JSON TO AZURE IOT" + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
6400 PRINT RJSON$
6500 FOR DATAINDEX% = 1 TO LENGTH%
6600 OUT 31, ASC(MID$(RJSON$, DATAINDEX%, 1))
6700 NEXT DATAINDEX%
6800 OUT 31, 0 : REM TERMINATING NULL CAUSE PUBLISH TO AZURE IOT
6900 RETURN
